name: Selenium disulfide
lead: Selenium disulfide (selenium sulfide) is a topical antifungal and keratolytic agent used in shampoos for dandruff, scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor. It is better described as a mixture of selenium sulfide ring compounds than a single pure compound.[1][2]

It entered US medical use in 1951 and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[2] The best-known OTC product is Selsun Blue (1% selenium disulfide).[2] It is not first-line therapy for seborrheic dermatitis, with ketoconazole generally tried earlier.[2]

paras: Uses are dandruff, scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor.[2] Wikipedia reports that a 2015 review found limited evidence based on one trial, and that research on hyperkeratosis, scalp psoriasis and dry-eye conditions rests on small series or trials in progress.[2]

Reported effects with scalp use are infrequent: itching or burning, rash, hair lightening, orange scalp staining and a chemical taste. It can discolour nails, light hair, dyes and metal jewellery. Temporary diffuse hair loss appears in case reports but not in several large studies. It should not be applied to damaged skin, where absorption is higher; systemic selenium toxicity can cause tremor, weakness and abdominal symptoms. Use in young children is not recommended, and pregnancy and breastfeeding have not been studied.[2]
In the US, 1% is sold over the counter and 2.5% by prescription. In the EU only 1% is available, with Belgium, the Netherlands and Poland reported to have banned it. In the UK it is pharmacy-only.[2]

A 2022 study examined scalp microbiome changes and clinical improvement in mild-to-moderate seborrheic dermatitis using a selenium disulfide shampoo after initial ketoconazole treatment.[3] A 2023 review in the European Journal of Dermatology discusses it for rebalancing scalp microbiome and sebum quality in dandruff.[4] Registered studies include a trial of a 1% selenium disulfide and 1% salicylic acid shampoo on scalp lipids and water loss (NCT05503706),[5] and a randomised trial of 1.8% selenium sulfide versus 2% ketoconazole shampoo in pityriasis versicolor (NCT04007237).[6]

timeline.event: Introduced for medical use in the United States.[2]

card.summary: An old-school dandruff shampoo active (Selsun Blue); a scalp-condition treatment, not a hair-growth one.
card.note: Can stain light hair and jewellery; avoid damaged skin per labels.

quick.overview:
Selenium disulfide is an antifungal and keratolytic ingredient in dandruff shampoos such as Selsun Blue. It is used for dandruff, scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor.

It is generally regarded as a second option after ketoconazole for seborrheic dermatitis.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an antifungal against Malassezia and loosens scale as a keratolytic; the detailed molecular mechanism is not well described.
quick.risks: Scalp itching, burning, hair lightening, orange staining and discolouration of jewellery are reported. Absorption is higher through damaged skin. Strength limits differ by country.
